screens.title: Function Objects (Functors) and Lambdas
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we open the door on two complementary C++ techniques that make algorithm customization both expressive and efficient: function objects, often called functors, and lambda expressions. A functor is simply an object whose class defines the function call operator. That allows the instance to hold constructor-initialized state and behave like a callable. Lambdas are the inline, anonymous way to write small function objects right where you need them. You will learn when a small lambda is preferable and when a full functor with stored state is the right tool. We'll also cover std::function, the versatile type-erased wrapper that can hold regular functions, functors, or lambdas so you can store or pass them uniformly. Safety matters: capture modes control whether a lambda copies or references variables from its enclosing scope, and careless reference captures can cause dangling references when lifetimes don't line up. Through concrete examples — printing with an index, multiplying values, custom sorting, and a hands-on Student filtering task — you will see both patterns, common pitfalls, and best practices that return reliable, readable C++ code. By the end you'll know the trade-offs and when to reach for a functor, a lambda, or std::function.

screens.title: What is a Function Object (Functor)?
screens.narratorSegment: A function object, or functor, is a class type that overloads the function call operator so an instance can be invoked like a function. This simple definition is powerful because a functor can hold data in member variables that influence every call. That stored state is initialized via a constructor, and subsequent operator calls can read or modify it. For example, a print-with-index functor keeps a counter inside the object and increments it each time it is called, producing indexed output without global variables. Functors are therefore appropriate when repeated calls share context or when you want better performance than a type-erased wrapper. A common misconception is that functors are more verbose without benefits; in fact, for reusable or stateful callables they are clearer and can enable small, inlined optimizations by the compiler. Concrete example: a multiplier functor stores a factor and multiplies input values when invoked. When should you choose a functor over a lambda? Choose a functor when the operation needs persistent state, constructor setup, or when you expect to pass the callable to many algorithms over time. A quick question to consider: if your callable must own significant data or initialization steps, is an object with operator parentheses easier to test and reuse than a captured lambda? The answer is usually yes.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A functor is a callable object type that can carry state in members and be invoked via operator parentheses.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.4 › Definition
Definition & Analogy

Think of a functor as a small machine you build and hand to an algorithm. The machine remembers settings you configured in its constructor and acts the same way every time it is run.

Common uses
  • Counting calls or maintaining an index.
  • Applying a transformation that depends on a stored parameter.
  • When construction is nontrivial and you want reusable callable objects.
Key Takeaway

Use functors when you need persisted state and clear construction semantics across many calls.

Code Example
// A simple functor to print an element and its index
class PrintWithIndex {
private:
  int index_counter;
public:
  PrintWithIndex() : index_counter(0) {}

  void operator()(int n) {
    std::cout << "Element at index " << index_counter++ << ": " << n << std::endl;
  }
};

// A functor to multiply by a factor
class Multiplier {
private:
  int factor;
public:
  Multiplier(int f) : factor(f) {}

  int operator()(int n) const {
    return n * factor;
  }
};
Key Takeaway

Functors provide callable objects with constructor-initialized state that integrates cleanly with STL algorithms.

Common Mistake

Don't implement a full class for a trivial one-off; lambdas are often better for tiny tasks.

screens.title: Practical Functor Examples
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through two practical functor examples and how they interact with algorithms. First, the PrintWithIndex functor holds an internal index counter initialized to zero in the constructor. Each time the functor is invoked by for_each, it prints the element and increments the counter. That pattern avoids global state and keeps the counter local to the callable. Second, the Multiplier functor stores a factor as a member and returns multiplied values from operator parentheses. Passing a Multiplier instance to transform produces a new sequence without needing a separate multiplication loop. A misconception to avoid is thinking functors are always heavier than lambdas; for repeated operations with nontrivial initialization, a functor is clearer and may perform better. Consider lifetime: the functor instance you pass into an algorithm must remain valid for the duration of the call; typically you pass a temporary or a named object at call time and the algorithm invokes it immediately. Concrete walkthrough: construct a Multiplier with factor five, pass it to std::transform with input and output ranges, then iterate the output to verify values. This pattern composes cleanly and separates construction from application. Closing question: when your callable needs a one-time small capture versus ongoing state, which approach will keep your code clearer and why?

keyIdea.text: Use functors when you want constructor-based configuration and repeated invocation with shared, local state.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.4 › Process Flow
Walkthrough: PrintWithIndex

Create the object, then pass it to std::for_each. The object's state persists across each call from the algorithm until the call completes.

#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>

std::vector<int> numbers = {1,2,3,4,5};
std::for_each(numbers.begin(), numbers.end(), PrintWithIndex());
Example output shows the index increasing for each element. The counter lives in the functor, not globally.
Walkthrough: Multiplier + std::transform

Construct a Multiplier with a factor and pass it to transform to produce a multiplied sequence. The functor's factor is configured once at construction.

std::vector<int> input = {1,2,3,4,5};
std::vector<int> output(input.size());
Multiplier multiplyBy5(5);
std::transform(input.begin(), input.end(), output.begin(), multiplyBy5);
// output now holds 5,10,15,20,25
Key Takeaway

Functor construction separates setup from repeated invocation, making code explicit and testable.

Pro Tip

If the operation is used only once in place, prefer a lambda for brevity; if reused, prefer a functor.

screens.title: Lambda Expressions: Syntax and Purpose
screens.narratorSegment: Lambdas give you a compact way to write function objects directly where you need them. The basic structure has a capture list, parameter list, optional return specification, and body. The capture list determines which variables from the surrounding scope the lambda can access and whether those variables are copied or referenced. For example, capturing a simple integer by value creates a private copy inside the lambda; capturing by reference binds the lambda to the original variable. Lambdas shine with STL algorithms because you can define sorting criteria, transformation logic, or simple printing behavior right at the call site, reducing indirection and improving readability. A common misconception is that lambdas are unsafe; they are safe when you choose captures that match the lambda's lifetime. Use value capture for short-lived lambdas that may outlive the original scope, and prefer explicit captures like [factor] or [&index] instead of blanket [=] or [&] unless you are certain. Practice reading a lambda by asking: what is captured, how is it accessed, and will the lambda outlive the captured variables? Conclude by trying a short example: a lambda that multiplies by a captured factor passed to std::transform — compact and immediately understandable.

keyIdea.title: Lambda purpose
keyIdea.text: Lambdas are inline anonymous callables with explicit capture controls for concise algorithm customization.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.4 › Definition
Lambda Anatomy
Capture List
Controls which external variables the lambda can access and whether by value or by reference.
Parameters & Return
Parameters are regular; return type is optional and often deduced by the compiler.
Readability tip

Prefer explicit captures like [factor] or [&index] to make dependencies clear at a glance.

Code Examples
// Capture factor by value
int factor = 5;
std::transform(nums.begin(), nums.end(), out.begin(), [factor](int n){ return n * factor; });

// Capture index by reference to modify it
int index_counter = 0;
std::for_each(nums.begin(), nums.end(), [&](int n){
  std::cout << "Element at index " << index_counter++ << ": " << n << std::endl;
});
Common Mistake

Avoid over-capturing with [=] or [&] unless you know exactly which variables will be used and their lifetimes.

screens.title: Capture Modes: Value vs Reference
screens.narratorSegment: Capture mode is the most important part of a lambda for safety and semantics. Capturing by value makes a copy of the selected variable when the lambda is created. This copied value will remain alive as part of the lambda even if the original variable goes out of scope, which prevents dangling references and makes the lambda self-contained. Capturing by reference gives the lambda a reference to the original variable; this is efficient and lets the lambda observe or modify the original, but it is risky if the lambda is stored or executed after the original variable's scope ends. Many bugs stem from accidental reference capture combined with asynchronous use. There are also the implicit captures [=] and [&] which capture all used variables by value or by reference respectively — convenient but easy to over-capture. A useful pattern is to prefer explicit captures and to use value capture for simple, small types when the lambda might outlive the context. A concrete contrasting example: capturing an integer threshold by value for a short-lived filter is safe and cheap; capturing a reference to a local container that will be destroyed leads to undefined behavior. To test your understanding, ask yourself: will this lambda be stored or run later? If yes, prefer value capture or copy the necessary data into a safe owning object first.

keyIdea.text: Value capture favors safety and self-containment; reference capture favors performance and shared mutation but risks dangling references when lifetimes mismatch.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.4 › Comparison
Capture by Value
  • Makes a copy at lambda creation time.
  • Makes the lambda self-contained and safe across scopes.
  • Good for small, cheap-to-copy types like ints or small structs.
double minScore = 85.0;
auto new_end = std::remove_if(v.begin(), v.end(), [minScore](const Student& s){
  return s.score < minScore;
});
Capture by Reference
  • Binds directly to the original variable; no copy is made.
  • Efficient and allows mutation of the original.
  • Risky if the lambda outlives the original variable: dangling reference hazard.
int index = 0;
std::for_each(v.begin(), v.end(), [&](int n){
  std::cout << "Element " << index++ << ": " << n << std::endl;
});
Rule of Thumb
If a lambda is stored or used asynchronously, prefer value capture for safety.
Misconception Check
Reference capture is not always faster; copying small types is cheap and safer.
Quick Question
Will this lambda be used after the current function returns? If yes, avoid [&].

screens.title: Mutable Lambdas and Captured Copies
screens.narratorSegment: By default, values captured by value are const inside a lambda. That prevents accidental modification of the captured copy, which is often desirable. When you need to modify the captured copy across invocations of that lambda, mark the lambda mutable. Mutable creates a non-const call operator on the generated closure type, allowing you to modify the captured copy inside the lambda body. A typical use is an incrementing counter captured by value so the lambda updates its private copy each time it is called but does not change the original variable in the surrounding scope. For example, capturing counter by value and declaring mutable lets the lambda increment its copy for internal bookkeeping. A common pitfall is expecting the original variable to change; it will not. The original remains unchanged because the lambda modified only its internal copy. If you need shared mutation visible outside, capture by reference instead. Consider lifetime and intent: use mutable when the lambda owns its private state and you want to modify that internal state across calls. As a closing thought, always document why you chose mutable so future readers don't expect a different effect.

keyIdea.title: Mutable
keyIdea.text: mutable lets a lambda modify its captured-by-value copies, but it does not affect the original variables outside the lambda.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.4 › Definition
When to use mutable

Use mutable when the lambda should keep and update its own internal copy between invocations while leaving the original variable unchanged.

int counter = 0;
auto incrementer = [counter]() mutable {
  counter++; // modifies the captured copy inside the closure
  std::cout << "Counter: " << counter << std::endl;
};

incrementer(); // prints 1
incrementer(); // prints 2
// original 'counter' remains 0
Notes & Pitfalls
  • Mutable affects the closure's copy, not the outer variable.
  • Prefer explicit intent: use mutable only when you mean to own the copy.
Pro Tip

If you need shared mutation, capture by reference and document the reason clearly.

screens.title: std::function: A Generic Callable Wrapper
screens.narratorSegment: std::function is a type-erased wrapper that can hold any callable target with a matching signature: a normal function pointer, a functor instance, or a lambda. That makes it valuable for APIs that accept callbacks or for containers that need to store heterogeneous callables. Use std::function when you need uniform storage or a polymorphic interface for callables. The trade-off is that type erasure introduces a small runtime cost and potential allocation overhead; for performance-critical inner loops prefer concrete types or templates. Concretely, you can assign a regular function, a functor, or a lambda into a std::function object and then invoke it as if it were a function. This is convenient for implementing command patterns, callbacks, or plugin-style extensibility. A common misconception is that std::function replaces lambdas and functors; instead, it complements them by providing a uniform handle when you need one. If you need maximum performance and the callable type is known at compile time, prefer templates or direct passing. When you need flexibility and storage, prefer std::function. Closing reflection: when designing an A P I that accepts external behavior, ask whether you prefer the flexibility of std::function or the performance guarantees of templates.

keyIdea.title: std::function
keyIdea.text: A type-erasing wrapper that can hold functions, functors, or lambdas for uniform storage and invocation.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.4 › Definition
Why use std::function

It lets you accept or store any callable with a matching signature. This is especially useful for callbacks or plugin-style extension points.

#include <functional>
int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }

std::function<int(int,int)> op1 = add;            // function
std::function<int(int,int)> op2 = Subtract();    // functor
std::function<int(int,int)> op3 = [](int a,int b){ return a*b; }; // lambda
Trade-offs
  • Convenience and uniformity vs small runtime cost and possible allocation.
  • Prefer std::function for API-level flexibility; prefer templates for hot loops when type is known.
Key Takeaway

std::function trades compile-time type knowledge for runtime flexibility, ideal for callbacks and polymorphic storage.

screens.title: Using Lambdas with STL Algorithms
screens.narratorSegment: Lambdas become especially powerful when paired with STL algorithms. Use std::transform with a lambda to create a transformed output sequence without explicit loops. Use std::for_each to apply side-effecting operations like printing formatted output. Use std::sort with a lambda comparator to express custom ordering concisely. For example, to multiply numbers by a captured factor, capture factor by value in the lambda passed to transform; this is compact and expresses intent clearly. To print elements with an index, capture an external index by reference so the lambda can increment it as for_each visits elements. To sort strings by length, provide a comparator lambda that returns whether one length is less than another. A common mistake is using reference capture with lambdas that are stored or used after the enclosing scope: that leads to undefined behavior. Another practical concern is that remove_if only reorders elements and returns a new end; you must call erase with the returned iterator to actually remove elements from the container. A final practical tip: readability matters — prefer clear, small lambdas over dense, multi-line bodies hidden in algorithm calls. That helps maintenance and reduces mistakes in capture choices.

Module 05 › Chapter 5.4 › Code Walkthrough
Transform with Lambda
int factor = 5;
std::transform(numbers.begin(), numbers.end(), out.begin(), [factor](int n){
  return n * factor;
});
Value capture is appropriate here because the lambda is used immediately and a copy of factor is cheap.
Sort and For_each
// Sort by string length
std::sort(words.begin(), words.end(), [](const std::string& a, const std::string& b){
  return a.length() < b.length();
});

// Print formatted output
std::for_each(students.begin(), students.end(), [](const Student& s){
  std::cout << "Student ID: " << s.id << ", Name: " << s.name << std::endl;
});
Key Takeaway

Compose small lambdas with algorithms to express transformations and side effects succinctly, but always confirm capture safety.

screens.title: Dangling References: The Real Risk
screens.narratorSegment: A dangling reference occurs when a lambda stores a reference to a variable that no longer exists. This typically happens when you capture a local variable by reference, store the lambda in an object or return it, and then call it after the original function has returned. The referenced memory has been reclaimed, so using it produces undefined behavior. The chapter shows a clear example: a function creates a local integer and returns a lambda that captures it by reference. When the caller invokes the returned lambda, the reference points to non-existent storage. The safe alternatives are to capture by value so the lambda owns a copy, or to ensure the referenced object outlives the lambda by using a stable, long-lived container or heap allocation with controlled ownership. When designing callbacks or storing lambdas in std::function, always ask whether captured variables will survive as long as the callable. Misunderstanding this is a common source of subtle bugs. A practical diagnostic: if you see non-deterministic output or crashes after refactoring to store lambdas, inspect capture modes for reference captures to temporaries or locals that may have gone out of scope.

Module 05 › Chapter 5.4 › Definition
Danger Example
std::function<void()> create_lambda() {
  int x = 10;
  return [&]() { std::cout << x << std::endl; }; // captures x by reference
}

int main() {
  auto bad_lambda = create_lambda();
  // calling bad_lambda here would access a dangling reference
}
Safer Alternatives
  • Capture by value to make the lambda own a copy.
  • Ensure referenced objects outlive stored callables.
  • Prefer explicit captures to make ownership clear.
Common Bug

Storing a lambda that references locals is a frequent source of subtle crashes and non-deterministic behavior.

screens.title: Hands-on Activity: Students — Sort, Filter, Transform
screens.narratorSegment: This activity walks through a practical Student example that ties together sorting, filtering, and formatted output. Start with a Student struct containing name, id, and score. Populate a vector with at least five sample students. Step one is to sort students by score in descending order using std::sort with a comparator lambda that compares scores. Step two is filtering: choose a minimum score threshold and use std::remove_if with a lambda that captures the threshold by value to move below-threshold students to the end. Call erase with the returned iterator to remove those elements permanently. Step three is transform or for_each to print formatted output; use a lambda that reads student fields and prints an ID and name. Important checks: capture the minScore by value to avoid lifetime issues and remember remove_if does not actually erase elements until you call erase. A common misconception is thinking remove_if itself shrinks the container; it only rearranges elements. As you implement, test each step by printing intermediate results so you can confirm sort order and the effect of filtering. This step-by-step practice demonstrates conclusion: lambdas let you express each algorithmic step clearly and compositionally.

screens.title: Best Practices and Common Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Summarizing best practices helps you choose the right approach. Prefer small, focused lambdas for inline, one-off behavior. Prefer functors when you need constructor-based setup, repeated use, or clearer testability for complex callables. When an A P I needs to accept many different callable types, std::function is appropriate for uniform storage, but be mindful of its runtime cost. Always favor explicit captures over blanket [=] or [&] to make dependencies obvious. For lifetimes: if a callable may be stored or used outside the creating scope, capture necessary data by value or otherwise ensure the captured object outlives the callable. Mutable should be used sparingly and with clear intent, because it changes the expectations about whether outer variables are affected. Watch for the remove_if erase pattern: remove_if alone does not shrink containers. Finally, test behavior incrementally and print intermediate results when refactoring captures or switching between functor and lambda forms. A helpful rule: write the simplest thing that works, then make the ownership explicit. That gives both clear code and predictable runtime behavior. Best Practices and Common Pitfalls means favor clarity: explicit captures, testable functors for complex state, and std::function only when you need runtime polymorphism of callables.. In practical terms, design choices: readability, safety, and performance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Readability

A functor is simply an object whose class defines the function call operator. That allows the instance to hold constructor-initialized state and behave like a callable. Lambdas are the inline, anonymous way to write small function objects right where you need them. You will learn when a small lambda is preferable and when a full functor with stored state is the right tool. We'll also cover std::function, the versatile type-erased wrapper that can hold regular functions, functors, or lambdas so you can store or pass them uniformly. Safety matters: capture modes control whether a lambda copies or references variables from its enclosing scope, and careless reference captures can cause dangling references when lifetimes don't line up. Through concrete examples — printing with an index, multiplying values, custom sorting, and a hands-on Student filtering task — you will see both patterns, common pitfalls, and best practices that return reliable, readable C++ code. By the end you'll know the trade-offs and when to reach for a functor, a lambda, or std::function.

Over the next screens you will build concrete skills that let you customize STL algorithms in safe, readable ways. First, you will define and implement function objects that overload the function call operator. This teaches you how to store constructor-initialized state and reuse logic across many calls, which matters when an operation needs context. Second, you will learn to use std::function as a type-erased wrapper so you can store different callable types interchangeably — useful for callbacks or command patterns. Third, you will study lambda syntax and capture modes so you can write concise, inline behavior and understand how captured variables are accessed. Fourth, you'll apply lambdas with algorithms like sort, transform, remove_if, and for_each, practicing idiomatic usage. Each objective is paired with a short explanation and a small mnemonic to help you remember when to choose a functor, a lambda, or std::function. These skills together let you write expressive, maintainable C++ code that leverages the power of the STL.

These next objectives focus on practice and safety. You will learn to write stateful functors for repeated use cases where a persistent counter or multiplier is required, and you'll contrast them with lambdas that capture state when a quick, inline operation is enough. You will practice the mutable lambda variant so you can modify a captured-by-value copy inside the lambda without altering the original. You will also learn to reason about dangling references and decide when to capture by value to keep a callable independent of the original scope. Finally, you will practise a hands-on Student filtering and sorting activity that combines sort, remove_if and for_each; that activity reveals lifetime, copying, and algorithmic patterns and reinforces the best practice of explicit captures. Each objective card includes a short why-it-matters note and a mnemonic to help you pick a safe capture strategy when writing real code.

A function object, or functor, is a class type that overloads the function call operator so an instance can be invoked like a function. This simple definition is powerful because a functor can hold data in member variables that influence every call. That stored state is initialized via a constructor, and subsequent operator calls can read or modify it. For example, a print-with-index functor keeps a counter inside the object and increments it each time it is called, producing indexed output without global variables. Functors are therefore appropriate when repeated calls share context or when you want better performance than a type-erased wrapper. A common misconception is that functors are more verbose without benefits; in fact, for reusable or stateful callables they are clearer and can enable small, inlined optimizations by the compiler. Concrete example: a multiplier functor stores a factor and multiplies input values when invoked. When should you choose a functor over a lambda? Choose a functor when the operation needs persistent state, constructor setup, or when you expect to pass the callable to many algorithms over time. A quick question to consider: if your callable must own significant data or initialization steps, is an object with operator parentheses easier to test and reuse than a captured lambda? The answer is usually yes.

Let's walk through two practical functor examples and how they interact with algorithms. First, the PrintWithIndex functor holds an internal index counter initialized to zero in the constructor. Each time the functor is invoked by for_each, it prints the element and increments the counter. That pattern avoids global state and keeps the counter local to the callable. Second, the Multiplier functor stores a factor as a member and returns multiplied values from operator parentheses. Passing a Multiplier instance to transform produces a new sequence without needing a separate multiplication loop. A misconception to avoid is thinking functors are always heavier than lambdas; for repeated operations with nontrivial initialization, a functor is clearer and may perform better. Consider lifetime: the functor instance you pass into an algorithm must remain valid for the duration of the call; typically you pass a temporary or a named object at call time and the algorithm invokes it immediately. Concrete walkthrough: construct a Multiplier with factor five, pass it to std::transform with input and output ranges, then iterate the output to verify values. This pattern composes cleanly and separates construction from application. Closing question: when your callable needs a one-time small capture versus ongoing state, which approach will keep your code clearer and why?

Lambdas give you a compact way to write function objects directly where you need them. The basic structure has a capture list, parameter list, optional return specification, and body. The capture list determines which variables from the surrounding scope the lambda can access and whether those variables are copied or referenced. For example, capturing a simple integer by value creates a private copy inside the lambda; capturing by reference binds the lambda to the original variable. Lambdas shine with STL algorithms because you can define sorting criteria, transformation logic, or simple printing behavior right at the call site, reducing indirection and improving readability. A common misconception is that lambdas are unsafe; they are safe when you choose captures that match the lambda's lifetime. Use value capture for short-lived lambdas that may outlive the original scope, and prefer explicit captures like [factor] or [&index] instead of blanket [=] or [&] unless you are certain. Practice reading a lambda by asking: what is captured, how is it accessed, and will the lambda outlive the captured variables? Conclude by trying a short example: a lambda that multiplies by a captured factor passed to std::transform — compact and immediately understandable.

Capture mode is the most important part of a lambda for safety and semantics. Capturing by value makes a copy of the selected variable when the lambda is created. This copied value will remain alive as part of the lambda even if the original variable goes out of scope, which prevents dangling references and makes the lambda self-contained. Capturing by reference gives the lambda a reference to the original variable; this is efficient and lets the lambda observe or modify the original, but it is risky if the lambda is stored or executed after the original variable's scope ends.
